latest_articles.title: Twitter Conversations: Gendered Issue Publics Among Women
latest_articles.abstract: We investigate how gender shapes women’s political discussion on Twitter using an issue publics framework. We test whether the conditions for gendered issue publics to form among women around feminine issues exist using data on political discussion via social media in the 2020 and 2022 elections. Our data includes political discussion among political candidates, elites, and non-elites, or regular people. Our results reveal several key findings. First, we find that men elites were more likely to discuss feminine issues, such as health care, compared to women elites, but we found no gender differences between regular Twitter users in our sample. Democratic women elites are more likely to discuss equity-based feminine issues, such as equal pay, than Republican women elites, but we find no partisan differences among non-elite women. We also find no gender or partisan differences at the elite and non-elite levels in the discussion of trait-based feminine issues, such as education. Finally, we show that in 2022, the Dobbs decision that rescinded the constitutional right to an abortion in the U.S. increased the salience of this issue among both women and men. Overall, our research suggests that the conditions for issue publics among women may not strongly exist as we find that non-elite men talk about feminine issues too.
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, USA

latest_articles.title: Intersectoral capital movement and repositioning of television in the Indian media economy
latest_articles.abstract: With the growth of digital streaming platforms, the Indian media economy is witnessing widespread changes that challenge the business models of traditional media sectors. The article attempts to trace the overall movement of investment capital between the television sector and other sectors of the economy as a consequence of the digital transition. The study uses a combination of network analysis and qualitative analysis to detail a tectonic shift in the frequency and directionality of capital movement across two concomitant periods of remediation: digitalisation and platformisation. In the first period, television was the centre of capital inflow from other sectors, whereas in the subsequent period there was a repositioning of television as it became a centre of capital resources shifting to other sectors. This article argues that the logic driving these repositioning of capital derives from the perceived limits to growth in established business models and the redirection of advertising spend, a dilemma which arises from the underlying dynamics of revenue streams, competition for resources and a diversified national market.
affiliations: The University of Queensland-Indian Institute of Technology Delhi Research Academy, New Delhi, India
The University of Queensland, Saint Lucia, QLD, Australia
Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India

latest_articles.title: Open justice in the political economy of visibility: Governing the gaze in platform-mediated courtrooms
latest_articles.abstract: This essay examines how the principle of open justice is reconfigured under conditions of platform-mediated visibility. While openness has long been understood as a democratic safeguard, socio-legal and media scholarship shows that visibility is never neutral but staged, mediated, and institutionally structured. Positioned as a conceptual intervention into debates about media, visibility, and public authority, the essay argues that contemporary open justice operates within a political economy of visibility, in which judicial legitimacy is increasingly shaped by the infrastructures that organise how courtroom images circulate, attract attention, and generate value. Rather than focussing on courtroom access and transparency, the essay examines the conditions under which judicial visibility is produced, circulated, and monetised. Drawing on the 2022 Depp–Heard defamation trial in Fairfax County, Virginia, as an analytically revealing US case, it shows how such trials unfold within platform environments structured by algorithmic ranking, metricisation, and monetisation, where visibility functions as a regulated resource rather than a simple guarantee of transparency. The essay develops a conceptual lens for understanding how judicial authority is co-produced by courts, media institutions, platforms, and networked publics. It concludes that justice today is increasingly governed through the organised conditions of its appearance.

latest_articles.title: The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.
affiliations: Amsterdam School of Communication Research, University of Amsterdam, The Netherlands
Empirical Communication Research, Leibniz-Institut für Medienforschung Hans-Bredow-Institut, University of Hamburg, Germany
Strategic Communication, Wageningen University and Research, The Netherlands

latest_articles.title: When academic leaders disconnect from social media in Finland: Situational rationality, silent resistance
latest_articles.abstract: This qualitative study, conducted at Finland’s research universities, analyses high-profile academic leaders who have chosen to be disconnected from social media. We conducted individual interviews with 19 leaders and performed a situational analysis to investigate the rationale for abstaining from social media. Academic leaders rationalised disconnection by reasons related to personality, sociability, critical rationality, and health and security. The leaders’ intensive involvement in three social worlds intensified the individual rationale for disconnection and enabled the leaders to work successfully despite disconnection. These social worlds were research and science, sensitive academia, and insider networks in society. In the context of the managerial neoliberal university, its promotional communication culture, and competition for visibility, the leaders’ disconnection from social media has a dissident, resistant characteristic. The study contributes to prior research through its comprehensive approach to academic leaders’ operational environment. Future research should elaborate on the systemic approach to social media in universities.
affiliations: Faculty of Education and Culture, Tampere University, Finland
Department of Language and Communication Studies, Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences, University of Jyväskylä, Finland

latest_articles.title: Accuracy and Defense Motives: Exploring Types of Information Insufficiency in the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) Model
latest_articles.abstract: This study reconceptualizes information insufficiency as a goal-contingent construct within the Risk Information Seeking and Processing model. In multifaceted risk contexts, individuals confront health threats alongside challenges to deep-seated values and beliefs, producing different judgmental demands within a single risk event. Survey data from 858 Hong Kong adults show two distinct forms of information insufficiency, one oriented toward accurate safety judgments and another toward defending deep-seated values and beliefs. Each form is associated with distinct patterns of information seeking and processing. This study demonstrates how multiple goal-based information insufficiencies operate within the same individual in response to different judgmental demands.
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong, China

latest_articles.title: “Who benefits, who is left behind, and who controls the narrative?”: E-commerce livestreaming and digital gentrification in contemporary rural China
latest_articles.abstract: As China’s countryside becomes increasingly entangled with digital technologies, a new form of rural gentrification is emerging—one driven by narrative control, cultural commodification, and algorithmic visibility. This paper examines how e-commerce livestreaming reshapes rural space in contemporary China. Drawing on a multi-site case study approach, this study reveals that gentrification in the digital era is no longer imposed solely by urban elites but is increasingly enacted from within rural communities and mediated by digital platforms. This process arises from the intersection of algorithmic market logics, state-led rural development policies, and the aspirations of rural communities to balance tradition with monetization. We identify this process as “co-constitutive gentrification from within” and trace it through three mutually reinforcing dynamics: the symbolic economy of rural imaginaries, the material remaking of livestreamable space, and the revaluation of earthy rural labor. The findings contribute to a broader theorization of digital rural transformation, demonstrating that gentrification in China’s countryside is as much about who gets to tell the story as it is about who owns the land.
affiliations: School of Foreign Studies, Xi’an Jiaotong University
School of International Studies, University of International Business and Economics

latest_articles.title: Coherence through sedimentation: Temporal organization and emergent interaction in Danmaku
latest_articles.abstract: This paper examines how coherence and participation are accomplished in danmaku, a commentary system on Chinese and Japanese video platforms where user comments scroll across the screen and are time-stamped to specific points on the video timeline. Although comments are produced asynchronously, they appear synchronously during playback, creating what has been described as pseudo-synchronicity ( Johnson, 2013 ; Liang, 2021 ). Building on research in computer-mediated communication (CMC), the paper investigates how interaction in danmaku is organized through multiple temporalities: the time of video playback, the time of message production, and the time of subsequent viewing. Drawing on a dataset of educational danmaku videos, we analyze how comments become sequentially and thematically linked through practices such as noticings, choral clustering, and indexical reference. The analysis demonstrates that coherence in danmaku emerges through stigmergic processes of sedimentation: participants leave visible traces that persist and accumulate, gradually transforming the comment stream into an interactional infrastructure that future viewers orient to. Much like graffiti layered across a public wall, danmaku commentary builds into an accumulated record of participation that becomes integral to the video itself. By foregrounding these temporal and stigmergic dimensions, the paper shows how danmaku reconfigures audience roles, blurs distinctions between live and asynchronous participation, and extends participation frameworks, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of emerging digitally mediated interaction in asynchronous, distributed settings.

latest_articles.title: Divorce stigma on Weibo: A corpus-assisted social media critical discourse analysis of platform-mediated contestation
latest_articles.abstract: Despite rising divorce rates in China, the traditional “intact family” ideal remains hegemonic, subjecting children from divorced families (CDF) to courtesy stigma. This study investigates how this stigma is discursively constructed, negotiated, and resisted on Weibo, a leading Chinese microblogging platform. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, we analyzed 2989 comments on Weibo using BERTopic modeling and social media critical discourse analysis (SM-CDA). The findings reveal a deeply paradoxical discursive landscape. Anchored by the ideology of “neofamilism”, a dominant discourse employs predication and intensification strategies to assert the “complete” family as a non-negotiable norm. This ideal enables a “deterministic stigma” wherein CDF are represented as inevitably “damaged”, “incomplete”, and denied agency. However, these stigmatizing practices are actively contested. A robust counter-discourse utilizes negation and comparative structure to reframe the source of harm from the act of divorce to chronic marital conflicts, while a parallel discourse of empathy fosters affective solidarity and reconstructs positive identities of CDF through personal narratives. As such, we argue that Weibo functions not merely as an amplifier of traditional norms but as a critical site of discursive contestation, where the bottom-up discourse of lived experience leverages the digital democratization of discourse to contest top-down anxieties over family fragmentation. This study contributes to a nuanced understanding of digital discursive stigmatization and destigmatization in non-Western contexts.

latest_articles.title: Sabrina Gonzalez Pasterski: Postfeminism and the representation of Latina scientists
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines news coverage of the physicist Sabrina Gonzalez Pasterski (SGP) through the lens of intersectional feminist critique. Since attaining minor celebrity in 2016, SGP may be the most famous Latinx American scientist to this date, but one whose fame has been dominated by what Rosalind Gill calls the “postfeminist sensibility.” Performing content analysis on 69 news articles, this study finds that media coverage of SGP has predominantly fixated on her childhood achievements at the expense of her scientific work. Drawing on the work of Anita Harris, this study argues that the media’s double stereotyping of SGP as an “exceptional woman” and as a Latina “can-do girl” precluded serious interest in her research. Thus, in the case of Latina scientists, the harms of postfeminism go beyond its oft-noted political impotence: postfeminism robs Latina girls of scientific role models by covering Latina scientists frivolously. Considering a recent talk by SGP, I conclude by highlighting the need for intersectionality in academic discussions of justice in science and in representations of women in science.

latest_articles.title: A Unifying Guide for Action: A Practical Synthesis of National Academies Documents on Mis- and Disinformation (2020–2025)
latest_articles.abstract: The rapid spread of mis/disinformation has become a threat to public health. In response, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) produced nine publications on this topic between 2020-2025. This study qualitatively analyzes and synthesizes these publications to examine how approaches to misinformation are articulated across levels and sectors. The most recent, a 2025 Consensus Study Report, served as a reference framework; its 13 formal recommendations guided deductive coding of proposed actions across the remaining publications, with inductive refinement of emergent themes. As a result, seven themes emerged: 1) community engagement, 2) tools and techniques to counter misinformation, 3) communication, 4) social media and online platforms, 5) collaboration, 6) journalism, and 7) other priorities. Across these themes, approaches are distributed, but unevenly developed, across individual, community, institutional, and technological levels, involving a wide range of actors. Taken together, these publications call for practical, audience-specific communication strategies grounded in trust-building efforts, with genuine community involvement. Future work should evaluate the effectiveness of proposed approaches while considering the evolving regulatory, political, and social context in which misinformation persists.
affiliations: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
City University of New York (CUNY), New York City
Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health

latest_articles.title: The Meanings of News: How U.S. Adults Think About the Word “News”
latest_articles.abstract: This study explores the immediate, top-of-mind meanings audiences hold about “news.” Inspired by recent audience-centric approaches in defining news, we adopt a schema framework to investigate mental representations of the news concept. Using a national probability survey of U.S. adults, we employ a thought-listing exercise combined with a network analysis. Our findings paint a complex picture of news and its meaning today. We identify six distinct news schemas (i.e., clusters of co-occurring words) that correspond to different audience demographics, political ideology, and news consumption. The findings underscore that news is a dynamic concept with implications for journalism scholarship and practice.

latest_articles.title: Short Episodes but Fast Friends: Examining the Effects of Parasocial Relationship Quality on Mediated Intergenerational Contact in Grace and Frankie
latest_articles.abstract: No scholarly consensus exists on the amount of media exposure necessary to encourage social prejudice reduction; however, drawing on work on cross-group friendships, this study provides evidence that contact quality is instrumental for facilitating parasocial intergroup contact when the length of character exposure is held constant. In an experiment on intergenerational parasocial contact, young adult viewers were assigned to watch either a high or low contact quality version of Grace and Frankie, a sitcom about older adults. The episodes were identical in length. A serial mediation model shows that participants in the high contact quality condition developed a stronger parasocial relationship with one of the characters, Grace, experienced heightened intergroup dissonance, and expressed greater willingness to engage with older adults. However, this parasocial contact process did not occur for the other character, Frankie. These findings contribute to research and theorizing about mediated intergroup contact and the role of media exemplar typicality in the contact process.

latest_articles.title: Communicating Climate Change in Africa: Role Perception and Role Shifting among Environmental Journalists in Nigeria
latest_articles.abstract: The environmental beat in Nigeria, as in most nations in African nations, is primarily covered by general assignment reporters. The role conception and perception of journalists who cover the environment and strive to communicate climate change issues continually fluctuate as they navigate the tension. To enhance our understanding of how journalists communicate climate change in Nigeria, we conducted a survey of journalists who occasionally cover environmental stories and identify as environmental journalists (N = 50) across various platforms, including print, broadcast, and digital media. Our findings show that environmental journalists in Nigeria use a combination of traditional news reporting techniques, feature writing, and solution-oriented journalism. Journalists utilize visual aids and storytelling to captivate their audiences, believing that their reporting influences public responses or drives policy changes. The use of visual storytelling and advocacy-oriented narratives reflects framing strategies that could make climate change more relatable and actionable. This study asserts that Nigerian environmental journalists, motivated by a duty to inform and inspire action on climate change, employ a hybrid reporting approach that combines advocacy and fact-based dissemination. Nigerian environmental journalists act as mediators, translating and amplifying local environmental knowledge into public discourse by intentionally balancing objectivity with advocacy.

latest_articles.title: Welcome to the Calentón: How Puerto Rican Community Leaders Respond to Extreme Heat
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how community leaders in Puerto Rico respond to the growing threat of extreme heat within the context of colonial inequality and climate vulnerability. As heat events become more frequent and severe, they exacerbate existing challenges, including unreliable energy infrastructure and public health inequities. To explore how leaders understand and address this challenge, two listening sessions were conducted in May 2025 with 17 community leaders. Reflexive thematic analysis revealed three central themes: Narratives of Disillusionment, reflecting frustrations with government inaction; Climate Recommendations that are Misaligned with Puerto Rican Realities, highlighting the disconnect between proposed adaptation strategies and lived conditions; and Filling the Gaps: Community-Led Climate Action, illustrating how leaders mobilize local knowledge, cultural traditions, and natural resources to adapt. Findings demonstrate that community leaders serve not only as advocates but also as communicators and knowledge holders whose perspectives are essential for context-specific climate solutions. This situates Puerto Rico's environmental communication within broader Latin American traditions of community-driven responses to socio-environmental crises while highlighting links between environmental risk and colonial exploitation. Puerto Rico's political subordination to the United States adds a colonial layer shaping resources and governance, making community-driven education a crucial environmental and political strategy for collective action.

latest_articles.title: Joining Dialogic Stewardship with Relational Engagement: Advancing Donor Relations Theorizing with Faith-Based Nonprofit Organizations
latest_articles.abstract: Despite their significant presence in social services and international aid, faith-based nonprofit organizations have been overlooked in public relations scholarship. To bridge this gap, this study integrates dialogic stewardship and the devotional-promotional relational engagement model to examine donor engagement within faith-based nonprofit organizations. Through interviews with communication professionals from faith-based nonprofits, findings confirm dialogic stewardship practices and introduces faith-centered stewardship. This study also identifies a broader relational ecosystem shaping donor engagement, including a relationship with a deity. This study advances public relations theorizing on donor relations and provides practical guidance for nonprofits seeking to foster mutual and ethical donor relationships.

latest_articles.title: Is Digitization Turning the Inverted Pyramid Upside Down? A Longitudinal Analysis of a Hundred Years of News Storytelling
latest_articles.abstract: The inverted pyramid model for structuring news articles, according to which the most important facts are presented in the lead sentence, can be regarded as a cornerstone of journalism. In this longitudinal study, news articles from various German media were analyzed over a 100-year period. Automated content analysis was applied to a large corpus of German news articles published between 1924 and 2024 to detect whether the so-called 5W1H-questions were answered at the beginning of the news stories. We focused on the prominence of the concrete facts what, who, when, where, without coding for why and how. This was complemented by a qualitative analysis of semistructured interviews with journalists from three generations, to contextualize and interpret the longitudinal quantitative findings. According to the results, the news structure remained stable both in media practice and in journalists’ perceptions of how news should be structured throughout the twentieth century. However, in the digital era this news structure appears to be under pressure. The findings suggest that while the inverted pyramid model remained remarkably resilient across different political regimes of the twentieth century, its dominance has begun to fluctuate in the context of a shifting media ecosystem and probably new business models online.

latest_articles.title: Rainbow Fatigue: The Effect of LGBTQIA+ Corporate Social Advocacy-Communication on Organizational Legitimacy
latest_articles.abstract: Organizations increasingly communicate about LGBTQIA+ themes, especially during Pride month. However, such corporate social advocacy-communication (CSA-communication) about LGBTQIA+ communities is often received with skepticism, as the public tends to doubt the authenticity of such engagement. This can eventually influence the perceived legitimacy of the communicating organizations negatively. The current study investigates public perceptions of CSA-communication on LGBTQIA+ themes and tests the effects on perceived legitimacy. A 2×2 factorial mixed-method experiment with a CSR control-condition has been conducted among the general Dutch public (N = 895) that compares the effect of timing (during Pride vs. Valentine’s Day) and organization’s effort (words-only support vs. support including a donation) in LGBTQIA+ communication on perceived legitimacy. The legitimacy perceptions were measured both with closed items and an open-ended answer option. Surprisingly, findings indicate that CSA-communication involving low effort caused higher levels of legitimacy than when more effort was invested. Timing of the LGBTQIA+ event did not impact the perceived legitimacy. Notably, generic CSR-communication predicted higher levels of legitimacy compared to CSA-communication on the LGBTQIA+ theme. This effect could be explained by a significant moderation effect of (negative) attitudes towards LGBTQIA+ people. The quantitative findings are contextualized by a qualitative analysis of the answers to an open-ended question about legitimacy.

latest_articles.title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
latest_articles.abstract: Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.
affiliations: Department of Humanities, University of Strathclyde, UK
School of Social and Political Sciences, University of Glasgow, UK

latest_articles.title: From Screen to Store: Exploring the Reality TV to Influencer Pipeline on “Love Island”
latest_articles.abstract: This paper examines how Love Island: USA Season 6 integrates e-commerce, brand partnerships, and influencer practices into its narrative structure and digital infrastructure. Focusing on the shop the villa feature of the show’s app, we analyze how the series synchronizes emotional investment with consumer action. Drawing on qualitative content analysis of episodes, a walkthrough study of the app, and thematic analysis of branded social media campaigns, we argue that Love Island extends and accelerates reality television’s longstanding commercial logics through a coordinated media ecosystem that integrates e-commerce, sponsorships, and post-show influencer pathways. While earlier reality formats cultivated marketable personalities and branded selves, Love Island intensifies these practices through platform infrastructures that transform contestants into commercially viable lifestyle brands and encourage audiences to participate through real-time shopping and social engagement. Ultimately, we show that Love Island operationalizes a reality-TV-to-influencer pipeline.
affiliations: University of Cincinnati Blue Ash College, USA

latest_articles.title: Platform Authority on Prime Time: PBS’s Finding Your Roots and the Televisual Production of Genetic Truth
latest_articles.abstract: Direct-to-consumer DNA testing has rendered family secrets newly visible through platforms that translate kinship into databases, laboratory-derived genetic profiles, algorithmic relative matching, and quantified displays. This article examines how PBS’s Finding Your Roots imports these genetic profiles and platform outputs into a legacy broadcast format, staging reveal sequences in which probabilistic inference is transformed into publicly authoritative truth. Drawing on a constructionist discourse analysis of four episodes, the article shows how the program assembles genealogical certainty through an evidentiary montage that aligns documents, DNA visualizations, and affective pacing. Page turns, close-ups on percentages or surnames, and host-led narration function as televisual certainty devices, scripting how audiences should interpret and feel about non-paternity events, racial passing, and enslaved ancestry. The analysis positions Finding Your Roots as a convergence text that legitimizes genealogical research and platform authority through television form, while obscuring the infrastructural conditions under which genealogical “truth” is produced.
affiliations: Saint Mary’s College of California, USA

latest_articles.title: Platforms Reshape Embeddedness? Platformization and Bilateral Embeddedness of the Chinese Audiovisual Industry
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates the transformation of embeddedness relationships in China’s audiovisual industry during platformization. Based on interviews with thirty-five audiovisual professionals in the Yangtze River Delta region, the study finds that under the dual administration of both the state and platforms, Chinese audiovisual producers have developed a model of bilateral embeddedness. While they integrate into platform ecosystems for IP and promotion resources, they simultaneously “pretend to” embed in state-led clusters to obtain policy support, without substantive participation inside. This bilateral embeddedness highlights a new configuration of audiovisual production, where audiovisual producers strategically negotiate between the state and platforms to enable a gradual economic transformation during platformization.

latest_articles.title: Student Athletes and Mental Health: A Social Identity Theory Perspective
latest_articles.abstract: Student athletes face unique stressors in comparison to both non-athlete students, and professional athletes. In light of mental health concerns faced by an increasing number of young adults, we examine the distinctive experiences of student athletes, and how these play a role in mental health issues faced by student athletes. We conducted focus groups with student athletes at two Division I institutions in the United States (n = 25). We analyzed our data through the lens of Social Identity Theory. Our findings highlighted the role of each component of the social identity theory—how they viewed themselves as different from non-athlete students (social categorization and social identification), but still competed with members of their in-groups (social comparison). This social competition suggests a singular experience of concurrently belonging to both in-groups and out-groups simultaneously, thus playing a role in their mental health.
affiliations: Shaheen Kanthawala (Michigan State University, 2019) is an associate professor in the department of Journalism & Creative Media at the University of Alabama. She researches health communication, social media, and other technologies

Jessica Payne (University of Alabama, 2025) is an assistant professor in the School of Communication at Illinois State University. Her research examines the intersection of media effects and sports communication, with a focus on connections among athletes, teams, organizations, and communities

Bree Holtz (Michigan State University, 2010) is a professor in the Department of Advertising & Public Relations and the Director of the Ethics Institute at Michigan State University. She is also an American Telemedicine Association College Fellow Dr. Holtz’s research explores the adoption, perceptions, and outcomes of telemedicine, mHealth, consumer-grade health sensors, electronic medical records, artificial intelligence (AI), and social media in health communication

Scott Parrott (University of North Carolina, 2013) is a professor in the School of Journalism & Mass Communications at the University of South Carolina in the USA. He researches the role of the mass media in shaping attitudes, emotions, and behavior related to mental health

latest_articles.title: Negotiating the platform turn: Genre, format, and co-production in RTP’s fiction strategy
latest_articles.abstract: This article investigates how Portugal’s public service broadcaster, Rádio e Televisão de Portugal (RTP), has adapted its fiction strategies over the past two decades, contrasting the pre-platform period (2005–2014) with the platform era following the entry of global streaming services into the Portuguese market (2015–2024). Drawing on platformisation theory and scholarship on small-market public service media (PSM), the study employs a mixed-methods, longitudinal approach, combining quantitative analysis of RTP1’s fiction output, qualitative content analysis of two series, and a semi-structured, exploratory interview with the programming director. Findings show that traditional pressures – such as limited budgets, small audience scale, and market constraints – were reconfigured in the platform era, generating both challenges and opportunities for innovation. Key strategies included a shift from horizontal to vertical scheduling, the increased production of medium-form series, an expansion of drama and crime genres, and selective transnational co-productions with global platforms. The study highlights how platformisation transforms content strategies in peripheral media systems, producing context-specific forms of constraint and creativity, and offers new insights into the adaptive capacities of small-market PSM in the digital streaming era.
affiliations: ULICES/CEAUL, University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal
imec-SMIT, Vrije Universiteit Brussels, Brussels, Belgium

latest_articles.title: Utopian media studies: Introduction
latest_articles.abstract: This introduction to the special issue ‘Utopian Media Studies’ sketches a framework for how media studies can become a site of utopian praxis, research and experimentation. It first addresses three apprehensions media scholars might have about the notion of utopian media studies and its appeal to a loaded concept like ‘utopia’. The introduction then outlines five sensibilities to explicate the nature and significance of this special issue’s contribution to the field: a utopian media studies must adopt an ecological approach to media; recognize and be invigorated by limits; work toward the technological liberation of time; connect imagination with practice; and emphasize and enable conditions for transmitting hope. Lastly, the introduction considers Ruth Levitas’s distinction between utopia’s archaeological, ontological, and architectural mode to map some of the concrete ways in which existing media studies research is doing utopian work that aligns with these sensibilities. In connecting work that operates in these modes with the various contributions to this special issue, the introduction reveals the utopian currents that already run through media studies as a discipline and opens up new conceptual and methodological approaches to studying and modeling digital utopias.

latest_articles.title: Gendering technology through lines and laughter: a critical analysis of the Turkish cartoon magazine Bayan Yanı
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines representations of gender—technology relations in everyday culture through cartoons in Bayan Yanı, Turkey’s first and only women-led cartoon publication, addressing an understudied intersection of gender, technology, and satirical visual culture in Turkey. It explores how humour-mediated cartoons construct gender—technology relations as a key means of expressing gender, both reinforcing and challenging gendered ideologies embedded in social and cultural structures, while shaping power dynamics within Turkey’s political and cultural context, where freedom of expression—particularly for women—remains limited. Adopting a qualitative case study approach, the study draws on a dataset of 82 images depicting women and technology from a ten-year archive (2011–2021) of the publication. The dataset was examined through thematic and visual analysis. The findings show that while traditional gender stereotypes persist, new forms of femininity and related myths are also emerging, reshaping contemporary women’s relationship to digital culture.

latest_articles.title: Understanding the Spanish manosphere through youth: an ethnographic study of young men’s engagement with masculinized online spaces
latest_articles.abstract: This article proposes a youth-centred approach to understanding the Spanish manosphere grounded in young men’s perspectives and experiences. Drawing on an ethnographic study with teenagers (between 14 and 18 years old) from Barcelona and its metropolitan area, we develop an analytical proposal that identifies three interconnected types of spaces: Open Hard Spaces, where explicitly anti-feminist and anti-LGBTIQ+ discourses are more visible; Open Soft Spaces, where stereotypically masculine content subtly reinforces gender hierarchies; and Close Peripheral Spaces, consisting of private peer interactions that normalize misogynistic practices and foster male complicity across online and offline contexts. Rather than offering a typology of the manosphere itself, this mapping shows how young men move and experience these fluid environments and how manosphere-related narratives are circulated, reinterpreted and normalized within their everyday social worlds. The findings highlight the need to understand the manosphere as a dynamic, fluid and relational media ecosystem that becomes embedded in youth cultures through peer-based interactions and seemingly non-political content, contributing to the normalization of toxic masculinity practices, perspectives and discourses.

latest_articles.title: Evaluating the impact of Work It Out Wombats! on children’s computational thinking and related skills in the United States
latest_articles.abstract: Computational thinking (CT) and related skills are important for children’s development and future success. CT can promote problem-solving and social-emotional learning (e.g. task persistence and frustration tolerance). Widely accessible educational media present opportunities for fostering the development of these skills in young children, especially those in historically underserved communities. Researchers conducted an 8-week randomized controlled trial with 458 children ages 4–5 from low-income households in the United States. This study explored whether providing access to educational videos and games for 1.5 hours per week supported children’s CT, problem-solving, and social-emotional learning. Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of two conditions and gave them internet-enabled tablets. Researchers instructed the treatment group to engage with videos, games, and activities from the CT-focused PBS KIDS series Work It Out Wombats! and told those in the control group to use any educational resources for the same period of time. Participants in the treatment condition scored significantly higher on a measure of sequencing skills at post-test, controlling for other pre-test assessments and demographics. We found no other significant group differences on post-test computational thinking, problem-solving, or social-emotional learning skills. We discuss the use of digital media to promote CT and implications for future work.

latest_articles.title: Fake news bargains in stakeholder perspectives and power dynamics: Equivalence framing of South Korean media
latest_articles.abstract: Fake news debates persist as competing evaluations of the same information problem coexist within news discourse. This study examines how fake-news response discourse is shaped by stakeholder perspectives and political dynamics in South Korean media. Using a quantitative content analysis of news coverage published between 2017 and 2024, the study analyzes pro- and anti-regulation responses and tests whether regulatory positions vary by ideological orientation, power ownership, and media partisanship. The findings show that pro-regulatory responses dominate the discourse, while stakeholder positions diverge between regulatory and nonregulatory approaches. Logistic regression results further indicate that regulatory attitudes are explained more strongly by power ownership than by ideological orientation, suggesting that shifts in ruling and opposing status shape regulatory debates more than stable ideological divisions. A slight variation, in which partisan media outlets featured politically contrasting actors actively endorsing regulatory stances, did not affect the overall outcomes, although it calls for further attention regarding media’s dual role as a press freedom safeguard and a sectarian stakeholder. These findings show how different regulatory evaluations are embedded in the complicated context of fake news discourse. By demonstrating this pattern in a long-term empirical setting, the study extends equivalence framing beyond experimental contexts and contributes to framing research by showing how enduring political conflict structures interpretations of fake news in journalism.
affiliations: Division of Communication and Media, Ewha Womans University

latest_articles.title: The hollowing out of local newspapers: A longitudinal study of journalistic performance decline and content homogenisation at a major UK publisher
latest_articles.abstract: The strategic restructuring of UK corporate-owned local newspapers through regional hubs has enabled content homogenisation across titles and centralised editorial operations away from communities, raising concerns about democratic commitment and place-based relevance in local news coverage. This study adapts an established framework for assessing journalistic performance — encompassing locality, originality, and coverage of critical information needs — to provide the first longitudinal evidence of how these dimensions evolve under organisational restructuring at Reach plc, the UK’s largest publisher. Using a panel of 27 newspapers across seven regional hubs observed monthly in 2019, 2022, and 2025, we find that: (1) local CIN content is declining while homogenisation intensifies; (2) homogenisation is applied primarily to lifestyle and geographically generic coverage, crowding out — rather than diluting — local CIN content; and (3) content shared within regional hubs remains markedly more local and CIN-aligned than group-wide content, which instead is largely lifestyle-oriented and non-geographic. Notably, regional hubs, once the main organising principle for content sharing, are losing influence to group-wide homogenisation — a trend coinciding with the creation of a national Content Hub and AI-assisted editorial tools. The findings point towards a downward trajectory in corporate-owned local journalism’s commitment to place and substantive coverage, with implications for community representation, democratic accountability, and media plurality policy, and contribute to a UK-specific theorisation of ‘zombie’ papers.
affiliations: School of Sciences, Psychology, Arts & Humanities, Computing, Engineering & Sports, Canterbury Christ Church University
Centre for the Study of Media, Communication and Power, King’s College London

latest_articles.title: Reworking Journalism at the Digital Periphery: Role Work among Political Creators
latest_articles.abstract: Political creators have become central actors in contemporary public communication and increasingly perform functions traditionally associated with journalism. Their growing presence has blurred the boundaries between journalism and its environment, raising questions about how journalistic roles are reworked beyond institutional newsrooms. Journalism studies have responded to these blurred boundaries through research on boundary negotiations, professional norms, and journalistic authority, largely from the perspective of the journalistic center. This article shifts the focus toward the periphery and examines how digitally enabled actors position themselves in relation to journalism and create their roles vis-à-vis the journalistic center. To conceptualize these peripheral perspectives, the article introduces the concept of role work and explores the concept in an exploratory empirical study. Drawing on 22 qualitative interviews with German political creators, the study shows that creators neither fully adopt nor categorically reject journalistic role models. Instead, they engage in selective, hybrid, and context-sensitive reinterpretations of journalistic values, goals, and practices. These processes of role work are shaped by platform affordances, small-scale production outside newsroom structures, the experienced boundary work of the journalistic center, and close, interactive relationships with audiences.
affiliations: Knowledge, and Communication, University of Augsburg

latest_articles.title: A Research Agenda for Studying LLM-Powered Persuasion Technology to Mitigate Misinformation
latest_articles.abstract: Emerging research on the use of large language models (LLMs) to counter false beliefs, including conspiracy theories, vaccine hesitancy, and climate denial, has relied predominantly on experimental methods rooted in social psychology, operationalizing persuasion as short-term attitudinal change measured through randomized controlled trials. We argue that this approach, while offering valuable causal inference, is insufficient for understanding how LLM-powered persuasion actually works. Drawing on communication theory and a qualitative analysis of publicly available transcripts from the “DebunkBot study” (Costello et al., 2024), we identify four constructs largely absent from existing research: users’ mental models of the LLM communicator, anthropomorphism (including negative forms such as attributions of naivety or gullibility that can drive resistance), folk theories about how AI systems operate, and epistemic literacy regarding machine-generated knowledge claims. We outline a research agenda organized around three priorities: methodological pluralism suited to the dynamic and personalized nature of LLM interactions, transparency and reproducibility standards for prompt design and transcript analysis, and ethical frameworks for assessing potential harms, including belief reinforcement among resistant participants and privacy risks in large-scale transcript data.

latest_articles.title: Hybrid Moderation in Practice: How Users, AI, and Professionals Judge Uncivil Comments
latest_articles.abstract: Online platforms increasingly rely on hybrid moderation systems that combine automated triage with professional human review, yet little research compares how these actors judge the same real content in production-linked settings. This article examines uncivil online comments as a platform-governance problem by comparing three decision-makers: registered users, a platform AI system, and professional moderators. Using a secondary dataset from a US-based publisher comment environment, we analyze real comments spanning five moderation categories: Violence, Doxxing, Hate Speech, Sexual Explicitness, and Personal Attacks. The dataset combines production-stage AI workflow dispositions, professional moderators’ final adjudications, and ex-post survey judgments from 863 registered users, yielding 8,588 user-comment decisions. Results show that users chose to allow publication of roughly two-thirds of the uncivil comments and that their decisions aligned more closely with the AI system’s publish-and-moderate versus hold-and-moderate orientation than with professional moderators’ publish-versus-block decisions. Divergence was concentrated in specific categories and items, especially Hate Speech. Users’ justifications suggest that permissive decisions often relied on threshold reasoning, rejection of toxicity, or free-speech concerns, whereas restrictive decisions more often relied on direct violation labels. Demographic and engagement-based predictors explained little variance in alignment. The findings suggest that users, AI systems, and professional moderators should not be treated as interchangeable moderation tools: they operationalize different thresholds and may be suited to different governance functions.

latest_articles.title: Resilience as a Structural Condition: Mental Health and Safety Challenges in Watchdog Science Journalism
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines resilience and mental health as structural conditions shaping journalists’ ability to perform a watchdog role in science-related domains. Based on 12 semi-structured interviews with Romanian investigative journalists, the study shows that watchdog science journalism operates in a fragile environment marked by institutional obstruction, financial precarity, harassment, and emotional strain. These pressures are particularly visible in investigations involving public health, environmental issues, and academic integrity, where journalists must deal with restricted access to information, expert authority, and public hostility. Participants describe burnout, anxiety, moral distress, and difficulties in sustaining long-term investigations without institutional support. Although they rely on coping strategies such as therapy, peer support, digital security practices, and professional networks, these mechanisms offer only partial protection. The article argues that resilience should not be understood only as an individual capacity, but as a structural requirement for sustaining watchdog science journalism. Understanding the conditions that undermine journalists’ mental health, safety, and autonomy is essential for assessing the democratic value of their watchdog function.

latest_articles.title: Transparency is a Double-Edged Sword: Stakeholders’ Perception of GenAI Usage Disclosure in Kenyan Newsrooms
latest_articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been increasingly adopted globally in journalism, raising critical ethical considerations, especially regarding the transparency of its usage in news production. Existing research shows that disclosing AI authorship or involvement in news writing affects news audiences’ perceived trustworthiness and credibility, with most studies conducted in the Global North. However, current research has primarily focused on news audiences, overlooking other key stakeholders, such as journalists and policymakers, who also shape ethical norms and practices surrounding AI transparency in journalism. Furthermore, research on GenAI in journalism remains heavily focused on the Global North, leaving significant gaps in understanding how stakeholders in the Global South perceive and evaluate GenAI disclosure in journalistic content. In response, we conducted 94 in-depth interviews with six groups in Kenya—news audiences, journalists, policymakers, influencers, journalism educators, and information technology experts—to examine how stakeholders in Kenya perceive GenAI disclosure in journalistic content and the extent to which they trust news stories generated by AI or assisted by AI. Our analysis shows a “double-edged sword effect”: While most stakeholders advocated for transparency about GenAI use in journalism, many journalists expressed concern that such disclosure could undermine the perceived authenticity and credibility of news content. Such distrust stemmed from ethical concerns that overreliance on GenAI could lead to “less human” journalism and the spread of unverified or biased GenAI content. Stakeholders also expressed conditional trust that varies depending on the type of story, the level of GenAI use, and the nature of the content.

latest_articles.title: When scientists ‘Tok: Memetic communication and scientific information engagement in short video-based social media
latest_articles.abstract: TikTok has rapidly emerged as an influential platform for science communication, particularly among younger audiences. Its affordances encourage memetic communication—characterized by imitation, humor, and participatory storytelling—offering scientists novel ways to engage publics. Our study explores scientists’ use of memetic elements on TikTok and their associations with audience engagement. Drawing on social media logic and platform vernacular theories, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 1025 science-related videos from 113 TikTok creators. Findings revealed widespread use of emotional and conversational language, but fewer videos incorporated reappropriated media or collectivist storytelling. Multilevel models showed that imitation and humor positively predicted likes, shares, comments, and views, whereas reappropriation negatively predicted engagement metrics. These results underscore the importance of aligning science communication strategies with platform-specific vernaculars. We discuss implications for public science engagement in digital, algorithmically driven environments, where visibility and audience trust increasingly depend on culturally resonant and participatory content.
affiliations: Center for Science Communication Research, School of Journalism and Communication, University of Oregon, Eugene, USA
Communication Research, College of Media and Communication, University of the Philippines Diliman, Quezon City, Philippines

latest_articles.title: Building DIY Coding Credibility: The Personas, Practices, and Pedagogies of Female AI Tech Influencers on YouTube
latest_articles.abstract: This article explores the instructional design practices of three female artificial intelligence tech influencers (AITIs) who use YouTube to teach coding and professional literacies. Our thematic analysis of nine video transcripts featuring generative AI (GAI) yielded themes centered on influencers’ persona development, flexible instructional methods, opportunities for application, and GAI limitations. We conclude the article by identifying a utilitarian ethical dilemma wherein AITIs avoid overt feminist arguments to reach a broader audience.

latest_articles.title: Grief-time in Wave 1.12.22
latest_articles.abstract: This essay responds to Desirée Rowe’s Wave 1.12.22. I read Rowe’s performance as an experiment in grief-time. Through a Black and women of color feminist reading of Rowe’s performance, I demonstrate the utility of grief-time, what it makes visible of our social landscapes, and consider it an equipment for living for other worldings.

latest_articles.title: Legal fictions and bodily realities: privacy, personhood, and the fall of Roe v. Wade
latest_articles.abstract: This essay reframes the conventional narrative of Roe v. Wade as feminist triumph and Dobbs v. Jackson as its reversal. Drawing on Elizabeth Bell's extension of Victor Turner's social drama model, I position Roe and Dobbs as intensifying performances of patriarchal redress. Roe's feminist progress rested on a constitutional compromise rooted in an exclusionary privacy doctrine. Those rights were secured, and simultaneously rendered vulnerable, from the outset. Bringing performance studies’ attention to embodiment, power, crisis, and redress into conversation with constitutional law, the essay exposes the limits of liberal privacy jurisprudence and the ongoing precarity of reproductive and queer rights.

latest_articles.title: Measuring perceived clarity: initial validity evidence from U.S. college student samples
latest_articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to develop a measure of perceived clarity. While various measures exist for assessing instructor behaviors that typically result in students perceiving clear instruction, there is no measure of the actual perceptual change in clarity. To address this gap, this study provides an initial validity portfolio for a perceived clarity measure through two studies. The results offer evidence supporting a 6-item semantic differential measure of perceived clarity, providing a tool for more accurate measurement practices in instructional contexts.

latest_articles.title: Sentence voice preferences and sentiment patterns in gendered Weibo headlines on violent events: A data-driven critical discourse analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on Fairclough’s three-dimensional Critical Discourse Analysis framework, this study investigates gendered language differences in Weibo hot-search topics related to violent incidents between 2021 and 2024. We combine quantitative textual and sentiment analysis with discursive and socio-cultural interpretation to reveal these differences, and to uncover the possible motivations underlying them. The quantitative results reveal a consistent preference for passive-voice constructions when men are the perpetrators and women the victims, possibly muting male agency and foregrounding female suffering. At the socio‑cultural level, the results illustrate how this syntactic bias can be sustained through the interplay of media conventions, Weibo’s algorithmic logic, and the reinforcement of traditional gender hierarchies. The multidimensional sentiment analysis finds no systematic emotion differences by perpetrator gender, which may partly reflect a tendency for some male-perpetrator headlines to adopt a more neutral and fact-focused tone despite the attention-driven nature of the hot-search system. This both aligns with the goals of upholding the media’s discursive stance, and reflects the prevailing social gender conventions. Our findings highlight the subtle but impactful role of syntax in demonstrating gendered power imbalances in social media discourse.
affiliations: Department of Linguistics, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China

latest_articles.title: Between Collaboration and Confrontation: Corporate Communication with Environmental NGOs
latest_articles.abstract: Sustainability is a pressing global concern, prompting corporations to engage with environmental NGOs (eNGOs) that scrutinize their practices and hold them publicly accountable. To explore how corporations shape their communication in these interactions, we conducted interviews with 13 Dutch communication professionals from targeted corporations. We identified three roles that corporations can take on – cooperative, confrontational, and silent – which are not mutually exclusive. Corporations may shift between these roles depending on the context, each associated with specific communication strategies. The cooperative role fosters dialogue, shared understanding, and collaboration. The confrontational role is primarily used in contexts of disruptive protest actions and climate litigation by eNGOs, where corporations clearly communicate their boundaries. The silent role reflects strategic non-communication in contexts such as climate litigation or high-visibility social media debates. By identifying these roles and their associated strategies, this study advances understanding of how corporations manage and maintain relationships with eNGOs while balancing openness, defense, and restraint.

latest_articles.title: Layered Censorship: Platform logics and the governance of taboo in religious Media
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how the governance of taboo issues is reconfigured across platformized communication environments. Drawing on a qualitative comparative analysis of the Walder affair—a moral crisis in Israeli Ultra-Orthodox society that erupted in November 2021 and culminated in the subject's suicide in December of that year—it analyzes how five distinct communication arenas managed allegations of sexual abuse against a prominent religious figure. The findings demonstrate that censorship does not operate as a unified institutional mechanism but as a distributed configuration of communicative practices. Different arenas adopted distinct modes of managing taboo information: institutional silence, normative enforcement, discursive displacement, selective disclosure, and contested openness. These variations reflect the communicative logics, institutional arrangements, and participation structures associated with different communication arenas. To account for these dynamics, the article introduces the concept of Layered Censorship: a platform-differentiated configuration of communicative practices through which taboo information is suppressed, displaced, selectively disclosed, morally regulated, and publicly contested across a shared media ecology. The concept highlights how different communication arenas perform distinct regulatory functions while occupying different positions along a continuum of discursive openness. By conceptualizing censorship as a distributed and differentiated form of communicative governance, the article offers a framework applicable beyond religious contexts to other highly regulated communication environments.

latest_articles.title: North Korean migrant women’s celebrity in South Korea’s platform economy
latest_articles.abstract: This article expands the analytical framework of post-feminism by situating it within a non-Western migratory context. Drawing on critical feminist approaches that conceptualise post-feminism as transnational discourse defining women’s subjectivities through neoliberal politics, the study examines North Korean migrant women’s self-representation within South Korea’s internet celebrity industry. It explores how post-feminism operates within the unique geopolitical context of the Korean division, emerging as a provincialised form of discourse shaped by vernacular gender dynamics and complex histories of marginalisation that transcend national borders. Specifically, the article presents a case study of Nolse Nara TV, a YouTube channel led by North Korean vlogger Nara. Employing feminist multimodal critical discourse analysis, the study investigates how Nara’s influencer identity aligns with post-feminist sensibility while tactfully navigating the intersections of gender, ethnicity, class and national identity. By examining the operation of post-feminism through this vernacular yet compelling case, the article offers broader insights into how its discursive and material power are further intensified for women whose marginality is historically grounded and politically charged. The article also calls for continued feminist engagement with self-representational practices of those whose social struggle has lost its political terrain in ever-expanding neoliberal politics.

latest_articles.title: Contesting Corporate Influence: A Comparative Analysis of Digital Audiovisual Regulation Under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement and Audiovisual Media Services Directive
latest_articles.abstract: This article compares regional legal frameworks regulating audiovisual streaming platforms in North America and the European Union. It examines the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) and Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD), focusing on their policy formation processes. Through thematic analysis of legal documents, media reports, and scholarly literature, the study identifies key provisions shaping digital audiovisual industries, the roles of interest groups, and the geopolitical factors influencing policy outcomes. By highlighting these contrasting approaches—free trade imperatives in the USMCA versus cultural and social priorities in the AVMSD—this article underscores how social power relations and regional dynamics shape streaming platform regulation. It positions audiovisual policy as a key site of contestation between free-market globalism and national/regional sovereignty, offering insights into the broader global implications of these frameworks.

latest_articles.title: Equally Credible? Examining Credibility Perceptions and Evaluation Processes of AI- and Human-Generated Information
latest_articles.abstract: As large language models are now capable of producing extremely humanlike content, it is crucial to understand how people assess the credibility of such information. Using Lee’s integrated theory of human-machine communication as a theoretical backbone, this study aims to examine whether information attributed to AI is considered equally credible as information attributed to humans and to identify the credibility cues used to evaluate each type of information. In an experiment, participants evaluated the credibility of news articles or social media posts labeled as AI- or human-authored as mostly equal, although human-authored social media posts were perceived as slightly more credible than AI-authored social media posts. Participants also evaluated AI- and human-generated information similarly in terms of how many and which credibility cues they relied on to make their evaluations. Importantly, prior AI attitudes did not affect participants’ credibility evaluations. The results are interpreted in the context of rapidly changing AI technologies and public experience with AI-generated content.

latest_articles.title: Infotainment on Social Media: Effects of Narrative, Dynamic, and Interactive News Presentation on Perceived and Actual Knowledge
latest_articles.abstract: News media companies increasingly create digital news content for Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok, thereby blending information and entertainment. Infotainment can enhance learning but might also lead to an illusion of knowing. We explore how the use of dynamic, narrative, and interactive features in Instagram stories affects perceived and actual knowledge about news issues. Two preregistered experiments were conducted: Study 1 (N = 124) compared different versions of digital news stories, and Study 2 (N = 121) additionally included a newspaper article as a control condition. The results demonstrate that the inclusion of dynamic, narrative, and interactive features in digital news items does not foster entertainment experiences and has no direct effect on actual and perceived knowledge. In Study 1, we found that infotainment features can increase knowledge for individuals who are less involved in a news topic; however, this effect did not replicate in Study 2.

latest_articles.title: Infrastructure Intermediaries: A Framework for Digital Infrastructure Research
latest_articles.abstract: Over the past 2 decades, scholars have turned their attention to digital infrastructures—the data centers, fiber-optic cables, satellites, towers, and interconnection facilities that carry Internet traffic—yet research on these systems remains fragmented across disciplines, institutions, and industries and siloed in specialized domains. This article introduces the concept of the infrastructure intermediary, arguing that media and communication scholars are uniquely positioned to mediate across the epistemic, institutional, and technological boundaries that shape infrastructural systems. Drawing on media and communication studies and adjacent fields, we advance an interdisciplinary framework for researching digital infrastructures in an era of climate disruption, artificial intelligence–related technological change, and regulatory uncertainty. The framework outlines approaches for infrastructure researchers to intervene collaboratively alongside affected communities, policy makers, and industry professionals, positioning scholars as active participants in building more equitable, sustainable, and just infrastructural futures. We close with an inventory of interventions for future research.
